Responses on the forced-choice item revealed no bias: Participants were about equally likely to report believing that nonbinary people are assigned female (48.89% of the sample) or male (51.11% of the sample).
Participants were undergraduate students recruited via an Introductory Psychology class in return for course credit.

Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select "slightly disagree" to an item requesting that response (n = 84; n = 22 did not respond to this item and were also excluded); (b) their participant identification number appeared more than once in the data file, suggesting they accessed the study multiple times (n = 45); or (c) their gender identity was not woman or man or their self-reported gender and sex did not coincide (n = 13; n = 28 did not report their gender or sex and were also excluded).
As in Study 1, participants were told the study examined how people think about different social groups and the researchers specifically wanted to know about their views regarding gender.

Specifically, participants completed two sets of three items asking separately about the perceived femininity and masculinity of the average nonbinary person, as follows: "Thinking of the average gender nonbinary person, how [feminine/masculine] in terms of [looks and physical appearance / interests and hobbies / mannerisms (for example, ways of speaking and behaving)] would you say they are?".
The two sets of items were presented in counterbalanced order and items within each subscale were randomized.
Participants next completed the same measure of attitudes toward nonbinary people as in Study 1 ( = .95, M = 5.23, SD = 1.30), provided demographic information, and were debriefed.foot_1

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Examining how respondents with diverse gender identities and sexual orientations think about the femininity and masculinity of nonbinary people represents a productive direction for future research. In all of the present studies, the goal was to obtain complete usable data from at least 250 participants, at which sample size correlations of the size typically observed in socialpersonality psychology stabilize (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013). The studies were made available to more than 250 participants due to anticipated data loss based on exclusion criteria. Some participants met multiple exclusion criteria. The final sample included 315 cisgender heterosexual U.S. participants (see Table 1 for demographic information), with N = 315 yielding 80% power to detect Cohen's d = 0.16 in a one-sample t-test (two-tailed, α = .05).

Data were collected during Fall 2024. Participants were undergraduate students recruited via an Introductory Psychology class in return for course credit. Study 2 was made available to 350 participants and was accessed by 351, not all of whom completed the study. Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select "slightly disagree" to an item requesting that response (n = 84; n = 22 did not respond to this item and were also excluded); (b) their participant identification number appeared more than once in the data file, suggesting they accessed the study multiple times (n = 45); or (c) their gender identity was not woman or man or their self-reported gender and sex did not coincide (n = 13; n = 28 did not report their gender or sex and were also excluded). Some participants met multiple exclusion criteria. The final sample included 216 cisgender primarily American participants (see Table 1 for demographic information). 3 A sample of 216 yielded 80% power to detect Cohen's d = 0.19 in a one-sample ttest (two-tailed, α = .05).

Data were collected in May 2025. Participants were recruited through CloudResearch Connect and each received a payment of $1. Participants were eligible if they had self-reported to CloudResearch that their gender was woman or man, their sexual orientation was straight/heterosexual, and they were U.S. citizens residing in the U.S. whose first language was English. Study 3 was made available to 320 participants and was accessed by 328, not all of whom completed the study. Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select 1 for demographic information). A sample of 277 yielded 80% power to detect Cohen's d = 0.17 in a one-sample ttest (two-tailed, α = .05).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps > .14", Text = "Ratings of competitiveness and passivity did not differ from the scale midpoint in either subsample (ps > .14)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 229 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.
#### Careless Responding

94 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **94 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Participants finally provided demographic information and were debriefed.

Responses on the forced-choice item revealed no bias: Participants were about equally likely to report believing that nonbinary people are assigned female (48.89% of the sample) or male (51.11% of the sample).
Participants were undergraduate students recruited via an Introductory Psychology class in return for course credit.

Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select "slightly disagree" to an item requesting that response (n = 84; n = 22 did not respond to this item and were also excluded); (b) their participant identification number appeared more than once in the data file, suggesting they accessed the study multiple times (n = 45); or (c) their gender identity was not woman or man or their self-reported gender and sex did not coincide (n = 13; n = 28 did not report their gender or sex and were also excluded).
As in Study 1, participants were told the study examined how people think about different social groups and the researchers specifically wanted to know about their views regarding gender.

Specifically, participants completed two sets of three items asking separately about the perceived femininity and masculinity of the average nonbinary person, as follows: "Thinking of the average gender nonbinary person, how [feminine/masculine] in terms of [looks and physical appearance / interests and hobbies / mannerisms (for example, ways of speaking and behaving)] would you say they are?".
The two sets of items were presented in counterbalanced order and items within each subscale were randomized.
Participants next completed the same measure of attitudes toward nonbinary people as in Study 1 ( = .95, M = 5.23, SD = 1.30), provided demographic information, and were debriefed.foot_1
Study 3 provided a replication of Study 2 among a sample of U.S. adults recruited from CloudResearch Connect (Hartman et al., 2023).
Participants were recruited through CloudResearch Connect and each received a payment of $1.

Participants were eligible if they had self-reported to CloudResearch that their gender was woman or man, their sexual orientation was straight/heterosexual, and they were U.S. citizens residing in the U.S. whose first language was English.
Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select 1 for demographic information).

The procedure was identical to Study 2 with three exceptions: Data were collected through CloudResearch Connect rather than from college students; the additional individual difference measures included in Study 2 (see Footnote 4) were not included; and just before providing demographic information, participants responded to the following open-ended question: "If you had to define gender nonbinary identity in your own words, what would you say?"

Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select "slightly disagree" to an attention-check item requesting that response (n = 34); (b) their CloudResearch identification number appeared more than once in the data file, suggesting they accessed the study multiple times (n = 17); (c) their self-reported sexual orientation did not match what they had previously reported to CloudResearch (n = 5; n = 21 did not report their sexual orientation and were also excluded); (d) they provided an incoherent response to an open-ended question (n = 8; n = 21 did not respond to this question and were also excluded); or (e) their Qualtrics reCAPTCHA score was less than 0.50 (n = 1; Qualtrics generates this score automatically and scores below 0.5 indicate possible bot-generated responses according to the Qualtrics algorithm).

info.title: FEMININITY AND MASCULINITY OF NONBINARY PEOPLE

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								University at Albany
								State University of New York

text.text: Perception of gender is ubiquitous and consequential in social life.
People who are perceived as women are expected to enact femininity, whereas people who are perceived as men are expected to enact masculinity.
How do gender nonbinary people fit into these binary assumptions?
The present work examined the perceived femininity and masculinity of nonbinary people.

In particular, cisgender primarily straight/heterosexual U.S.-based participants reported their assumptions about the assigned sex (Study 1; N = 315) or their perceptions of the femininity and masculinity (Studies 2-3; Ns = 216 and 277) of the average nonbinary person.
No apparent bias in terms of assumed sex or perceived femininity emerged, yet participants rated the average nonbinary person as reliably below the scale midpoint on masculinity.
Accordingly, straight cisgender Americans' perceptions of the average nonbinary person may in part reflect a tendency to safeguard masculinity.

Binary conceptions of gender permeate how people think about one another, often in ways that conflate gender identity (identification with a specific gender) with sex (classification typically as female or male according to physical attributes; Hyde et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Binary conceptions of gender permeate how people think about one another, often in ways that conflate gender identity (identification with a specific gender) with sex (classification typically as female or male according to physical attributes; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hyde et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, many believe that gender identity is determined by sex and therefore everyone must be a woman or a man (Saguy et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In particular, many believe that gender identity is determined by sex and therefore everyone must be a woman or a man <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Saguy et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Differences between women and men are considered fundamentally informative (Prentice & Miller, 2006), and women and men tend to occupy distinct social and occupational roles (Eagly & Wood, 2012), which informs stereotypes associated with each gender: Women are stereotypically associated with communal traits and men with agentic traits (Eagly et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Differences between women and men are considered fundamentally informative <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Prentice & Miller, 2006)</ref>, and women and men tend to occupy distinct social and occupational roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Eagly & Wood, 2012)</ref>, which informs stereotypes associated with each gender: Women are stereotypically associated with communal traits and men with agentic traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Eagly et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, not everyone conforms to such binary expectations.
Specifically, people who identify as nonbinary have a gender identity that is not captured by the woman/man binary (Hegarty et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Specifically, people who identify as nonbinary have a gender identity that is not captured by the woman/man binary <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hegarty et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: How do nonbinary people fit into the gendered assumptions that inform much of social life?
The present research addressed this question by examining cisgender Americans' perceptions of the femininity and masculinity of the average nonbinary person.
Nonbinary genders exist beyond, in between, or as a combination of the traditional gender binary of women and men (Matsuno & Budge, 2017).
text.formatted: Nonbinary genders exist beyond, in between, or as a combination of the traditional gender binary of women and men <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Matsuno & Budge, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Nonbinary gender is an umbrella term and nonbinary people experience their gender in diverse ways (Hegarty et al., 2018) -for example, as a mixture of woman and man (androgynous), a specific additional gender (a third gender), changing across time or contexts (genderfluid), or subverting binary gender (genderqueer).
text.formatted: Nonbinary gender is an umbrella term and nonbinary people experience their gender in diverse ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hegarty et al., 2018)</ref> -for example, as a mixture of woman and man (androgynous), a specific additional gender (a third gender), changing across time or contexts (genderfluid), or subverting binary gender <ref type="bibr">(genderqueer)</ref>.

text.text: Some nonbinary people identify as transgender (Darwin, 2020), and some use gender-neutral pronouns (Matsuno & Budge, 2017).
text.formatted: Some nonbinary people identify as transgender <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Darwin, 2020)</ref>, and some use gender-neutral pronouns <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Matsuno & Budge, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Approximately 1% of U.S. adults identified as nonbinary in 2022 -a figure that was higher at 3% among U.S. adults under the age of 30 (Brown, 2022).
text.formatted: Approximately 1% of U.S. adults identified as nonbinary in 2022 -a figure that was higher at 3% among U.S. adults under the age of 30 <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, about 11% of the U.S. adult LGBTQ population is estimated to be nonbinary (Wilson & Meyer, 2021).
text.formatted: Additionally, about 11% of the U.S. adult LGBTQ population is estimated to be nonbinary <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Wilson & Meyer, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The percentage of U.S. adults who know someone who uses gender-neutral pronouns increased from 18% in 2018 to 26% in 2021 (Minkin & Brown, 2021).
text.formatted: The percentage of U.S. adults who know someone who uses gender-neutral pronouns increased from 18% in 2018 to 26% in 2021 <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Minkin & Brown, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: According to data from October 2024, 23% of U.S. adults and 28% of U.S. teens report knowing someone who is nonbinary (Horowitz, 2025).
text.formatted: According to data from October 2024, 23% of U.S. adults and 28% of U.S. teens report knowing someone who is nonbinary <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Horowitz, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest a growing awareness of nonbinary gender in the U.S. However, relatively little is known about more specific perceptions of nonbinary people.

An increasingly large literature has documented the nature of attitudes toward transgender people (for a meta-analysis, see Hatch et al., 2022), which differ from those toward nonbinary people in important ways.
text.formatted: An increasingly large literature has documented the nature of attitudes toward transgender people (for a meta-analysis, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hatch et al., 2022)</ref>, which differ from those toward nonbinary people in important ways.

text.text: For example, transgender people face bias because they are perceived to violate the assumption that gender is determined by sex (Morgenroth et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, transgender people face bias because they are perceived to violate the assumption that gender is determined by sex <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Morgenroth et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Anti-transgender bias thus tends to take the form of denying gender category membership (e.g., the notion that transgender [wo]men are not "real" [wo]men).
text.formatted: Anti-transgender bias thus tends to take the form of denying gender category membership (e.g., the notion that transgender [wo]men are not "real" <ref type="bibr">[wo]</ref>men).

text.text: By contrast, nonbinary people may be perceived as eschewing the notion of binary gender (Croteau & Morrison, 2023; Johnson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: By contrast, nonbinary people may be perceived as eschewing the notion of binary gender <ref type="bibr">(Croteau & Morrison, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Johnson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Given that the majority of U.S. respondents report believing that gender is binary (Public Religion Research Institute, 2023), many perceivers may doubt the validity of nonbinary gender.
text.formatted: Given that the majority of U.S. respondents report believing that gender is binary <ref type="bibr">(Public Religion Research Institute, 2023)</ref>, many perceivers may doubt the validity of nonbinary gender.

text.text: Thus, bias against nonbinary people may be expressed as denial of the "realness" of their identity per se (Bartels et al., 2024; Valen & Burke, 2025).
text.formatted: Thus, bias against nonbinary people may be expressed as denial of the "realness" of their identity per se <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bartels et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Valen & Burke, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, attitudes toward nonbinary and transgender people should be examined separately.
Relatively few studies have assessed attitudes toward nonbinary people.

Cisgender people who score higher on gender essentialism, belief in the gender binary, endorsement of traditional gender roles, political conservatism, social dominance orientation, right-wing authoritarianism, and need for closure report more negative attitudes toward nonbinary people (Morgenroth et al., 2021; Perez-Arche & Miller, 2021; Schudson & van Anders, 2022; Valen & Burke, 2025).
text.formatted: Cisgender people who score higher on gender essentialism, belief in the gender binary, endorsement of traditional gender roles, political conservatism, social dominance orientation, right-wing authoritarianism, and need for closure report more negative attitudes toward nonbinary people <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Morgenroth et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Perez-Arche & Miller, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Schudson & van Anders, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Valen & Burke, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Compared to women and men, nonbinary people elicit less positive emotion, are viewed as less competent and lower in status, and their identities are rated as less "real" (McCarty & Burt, 2024; Valen & Burke, 2025).
text.formatted: Compared to women and men, nonbinary people elicit less positive emotion, are viewed as less competent and lower in status, and their identities are rated as less "real" <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(McCarty & Burt, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Valen & Burke, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present work sought to further elucidate how cisgender people think about nonbinary gender by examining how feminine and masculine cisgender Americans think the average nonbinary person is.
People are accustomed to making assumptions about others' gender and thus their femininity and masculinity as a routine part of social perception (Martin & Slepian, 2025).
text.formatted: People are accustomed to making assumptions about others' gender and thus their femininity and masculinity as a routine part of social perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Martin & Slepian, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Femininity and masculinity denote characteristics associated with women/femaleness and men/maleness that may vary by culture and time (Spence, 1984).
text.formatted: Femininity and masculinity denote characteristics associated with women/femaleness and men/maleness that may vary by culture and time <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Spence, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: People who do not conform to expectations about femininity and masculinity experience backlash.
For example, women who seem too masculine and men who seem insufficiently masculine elicit negative reactions (Moss-Racusin et al., 2010; Rudman et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For example, women who seem too masculine and men who seem insufficiently masculine elicit negative reactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Moss-Racusin et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Rudman et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, targets who appeared gender nonconforming due to engaging in gender-atypical behavior or based on facial appearance were misgendered and denied access to gender-appropriate spaces (e.g., bathrooms) regardless of whether they were cisgender or transgender (Morgenroth et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Moreover, targets who appeared gender nonconforming due to engaging in gender-atypical behavior or based on facial appearance were misgendered and denied access to gender-appropriate spaces (e.g., bathrooms) regardless of whether they were cisgender or transgender <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Morgenroth et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, individuals who do not fit neatly into specific binary genders and the associated expectations of femininity and masculinity are at risk of social sanctions.

Perceptions of nonbinary people represent an interesting test case of these established patterns: Although perceivers may lack strict gendered expectations for what nonbinary people should be like, backlash might nonetheless arise if nonbinary people are perceived as neither particularly feminine nor masculine (i.e., as defying the binary-gendered aspects of social perception; Martin & Mason, 2022; Martin & Slepian, 2020).
text.formatted: Perceptions of nonbinary people represent an interesting test case of these established patterns: Although perceivers may lack strict gendered expectations for what nonbinary people should be like, backlash might nonetheless arise if nonbinary people are perceived as neither particularly feminine nor masculine (i.e., as defying the binary-gendered aspects of social perception; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Martin & Mason, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Martin & Slepian, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this reasoning, it has been suggested that negative attitudes toward nonbinary people may stem from difficulty with matching them with preexisting gender schemas (Liebenow & Cassidy, 2025).
text.formatted: Consistent with this reasoning, it has been suggested that negative attitudes toward nonbinary people may stem from difficulty with matching them with preexisting gender schemas <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Liebenow & Cassidy, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: It is therefore important to understand how perceivers ascribe femininity and masculinity to nonbinary people.
Analogous to the diverse ways that nonbinary people experience their gender (Hegarty et al., 2018), several patterns of perceived femininity and masculinity are plausible.
text.formatted: Analogous to the diverse ways that nonbinary people experience their gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hegarty et al., 2018)</ref>, several patterns of perceived femininity and masculinity are plausible.

text.text: Cisgender perceivers might view the typical nonbinary person as low in femininity and masculinity (as agender); as high in femininity and masculinity (as bigender); or as neutral in femininity and masculinity (as androgynous).
Anecdotally, nonbinary gender is often assumed to be more prevalent among individuals assigned female (vs. male).
This assumption may lead perceivers to associate nonbinary people with femininity.
The present work explored whether cisgender U.S.
respondents' perceptions of the femininity and masculinity of the average nonbinary person match any of these plausible patterns.
In the present studies, U.S.-based participants self-reported their gender and sex, and data from only those inferred to be cisgender (i.e., whose gender coincided with their sex) were analyzed.
Study 1 examined assumptions about whether the average nonbinary person is more likely to be assigned female or male.
In Studies 2-3, participants reported the extent to which they thought the average nonbinary person is feminine and masculine and possesses traits traditionally associated with women and men.
I report all sample size determinations, data exclusions, manipulations, and measures, and no additional data were collected after analyses were conducted.
The studies were exploratory and not preregistered.
In Study 1, cisgender U.S. participants read a definition of nonbinary gender and indicated whether they thought the average nonbinary person is more likely to be assigned female or male.
1 Information on the association between nonbinary gender and assigned sex is limited.

Some data suggest the proportion of nonbinary people in the U.S. who are assigned female (vs. male) varies across generational cohorts, with Gen X and older nonbinary respondents being more likely to be male, millennials being equally likely to be female or male, and Gen Z respondents being more likely to be female (Twenge, 2024).

Examining how respondents with diverse gender identities and sexual orientations think about the femininity and masculinity of nonbinary people represents a productive direction for future research.

reported another type of relationship) Procedure and Measures Participants were told the study examined how people think about different social groups and the researchers specifically wanted to know about their views regarding gender.
Participants read the following instructions: "In this part of the study, we're interested in learning about your thoughts about people who are gender nonbinary.
Gender nonbinary people are individuals who do not identify as exclusively women/girls or men/boys.
Nonbinary gender is an umbrella term that includes many different identities that don't fit into the woman/man categories.
Some, but not all, gender nonbinary people use they/them pronouns; and some, but not all, identify as transgender."
Participants then indicated how familiar they were with the term gender nonbinary (1 = not familiar at all to5 = extremely familiar; M = 3.39, SD = 1.05).
Next, participants responded to dependent measures.
They first received the following instructions: "Gender nonbinary people have a gender identity that does not match the sex they were assigned at birth.
That is, gender nonbinary people might have been assigned female or male when they were born, but later in life they came to identify as gender nonbinary rather than as women or men.
With this information in mind, the next couple of questions will ask about your thoughts about whether gender nonbinary people are more likely to have been assigned male or female at birth."
Participants then responded to two items presented in counterbalanced order.

The forced-choice item read: "Thinking of the average or typical gender nonbinary person in the U.S. today, if I had to guess their sex assigned at birth, I would say they were…" (forcedchoice response options, presented in randomized order: female, male).
The percentage estimation item read: "Thinking of gender nonbinary people in the U. scored so that all data represented the estimated percentage assigned female.

Participants responded by typing in a number between 0 and 100 and received the following further instructions (as worded for participants asked to estimate the percentage assigned female): "0 would mean that 0% of gender nonbinary people are assigned female at birth (that is, all gender nonbinary people are assigned male at birth); 50 would mean that gender nonbinary people are equally likely to be assigned female or male at birth; 100 would mean that 100% of gender nonbinary people are assigned female at birth (that is, no gender nonbinary people are assigned male at birth).

In other words, numbers below 50 mean you believe gender nonbinary people are more likely to be assigned male at birth, and numbers above 50 mean you believe gender nonbinary people are more likely to be assigned female at birth."

Participants next completed a 14-item measure of attitudes toward gender nonbinary people (Morgenroth et al., 2021; e.g., "Gender nonbinary people should be accepted completely into our society";  = .97, M = 4.77, SD = 1.72).

text.text: Do cisgender U.S. perceivers think the average nonbinary person is more likely to be female or male?

Responses on the forced-choice item revealed no bias: Participants were about equally likely to report believing that nonbinary people are assigned female (48.89% of the sample) or male (51.11% of the sample).
A one-sample proportions test showed no reliable difference from 0.50 (i.e., equal chances of selecting female or male), Z = -0.39, p = .693.
Responses on the percentage estimation item revealed an analogous result.
On average, participants estimated that 50.74% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 48.86%-52.62%) of nonbinary people are assigned female (see Figure 1).

text.text: A one-sample t-test showed no reliable difference from 50%, t(314) = 0.77, p = .440, d = 0.04.

Of note, participants who reported more positive attitudes toward nonbinary people were slightly more likely to select female (vs. male) on the forced-choice item, r(313) = .12, p = .040, and estimated that a slightly larger percentage of nonbinary people are assigned female, r(313) = .15, p = .006.
Study 1 revealed no bias, on average, in cisgender U.S. participants' assumptions about the assigned sex of the average nonbinary person.
About half the sample reported believing that typical nonbinary people are female and the other half reported believing they are male.
Despite this lack of bias in terms of assumed sex, nonbinary people might be differentially associated with femininity and masculinity.
Study 2 explored this possibility.
Study 2 participants read the same definition of nonbinary gender as in Study 1 and indicated how feminine and masculine they thought the average nonbinary person is.
Participants also reported the extent to which they thought traits stereotypically associated with women (signaling communality) and men (signaling agency) describe the average nonbinary person.

text.text: Data were collected during Fall 2024.
Participants were undergraduate students recruited via an Introductory Psychology class in return for course credit.
Study 2 was made available to 350 participants and was accessed by 351, not all of whom completed the study.

Participants were excluded from analyses if: (a) they did not select "slightly disagree" to an item requesting that response (n = 84; n = 22 did not respond to this item and were also excluded); (b) their participant identification number appeared more than once in the data file, suggesting they accessed the study multiple times (n = 45); or (c) their gender identity was not woman or man or their self-reported gender and sex did not coincide (n = 13; n = 28 did not report their gender or sex and were also excluded).
Some participants met multiple exclusion criteria.

The final sample included 216 cisgender primarily American participants (see Table 1 for demographic information). 3 A sample of 216 yielded 80% power to detect Cohen's d = 0.19 in a one-sample ttest (two-tailed, α = .05).

text.text: As in Study 1, participants were told the study examined how people think about different social groups and the researchers specifically wanted to know about their views regarding gender.

Participants then read the same definition of nonbinary gender as in Study 1 and reported how familiar they were with the term gender nonbinary (1 = not familiar at all to5 = extremely familiar; M = 3.26, SD = 1.07).
Next, participants received the following instructions: "We'd like to learn about your general impressions of gender nonbinary people.
Even if you don't personally know anyone who is gender nonbinary, you may have an overall impression of what gender nonbinary people tend to be like.

In particular, we'd like to know how masculine (that is, having qualities generally associated with men or boys) or feminine (that is, having qualities generally associated with women or girls) you think the average gender nonbinary person is."
Participants then completed two measures -perceived femininity and masculinity and gendered trait attribution -in counterbalanced order.

Specifically, participants completed two sets of three items asking separately about the perceived femininity and masculinity of the average nonbinary person, as follows: "Thinking of the average gender nonbinary person, how [feminine/masculine] in terms of [looks and physical appearance / interests and hobbies / mannerisms (for example, ways of speaking and behaving)] would you say they are?".
Responses were made on sliding scales ranging from 0 (not feminine/masculine at all) to 100 (extremely feminine/masculine).
The two sets of items were presented in counterbalanced order and items within each subscale were randomized.
Items were averaged into indices of perceived femininity ( = .80) and masculinity ( = .80).
Participants also reported the extent to which they (dis)agreed (1 = strongly disagree to7 = strongly agree) that eight traits describe the average nonbinary person.

The traits came from work on descriptive (binary) gender stereotypes (Bem, 1974; Bhatia & Bhatia, 2021; Spence et al., 1975), which has established that four of them are associated with women/femininity (gentle, emotional, passive, kind) and four with men/masculinity (aggressive, dominant, independent, competitive).

text.text: Do cisgender respondents perceive the average nonbinary person as feminine and/or masculine?
Mean perceived femininity did not differ reliably from the scale midpoint of 50 (M = 51.10, 95% CI 49.08-53.12, SD = 15.06), one-sample t(215) = 1.07, p = .285, d = 0.07.
However, mean perceived masculinity was lower than 50 (M = 41.19, 95% CI 39.14-43.24, SD = 15.27), one-sample t(215) = 8.48, p < .001, d = 0.58.

text.text: However, an exploratory factor analysis with maximum likelihood extraction and Oblimin rotation revealed three factors with eigenvalues > 1.

text.text: The factor structure was difficult to interpret.
The traits gentle, kind, independent, and aggressive loaded on factor 1 (loadings of .85, .74, .55, and -.51, respectively).
Factor 2 consisted of three relatively weakly loading traits (aggressive, loading = .50; emotional, loading = .41; passive, loading = .38), the first of which loaded equally strongly on factor 1.
Competitive and dominant loaded on factor 3 (loadings of .60 and .52, respectively).
Thus, the pattern of trait attribution established in prior work on binary-gendered targets did not replicate.
Indeed, feminine traits did not form a reliable scale ( = .51), nor did masculine traits ( = .40).

Further analyses therefore explored the eight traits individually, with one-sample t-tests comparing their attribution against the scale midpoint (4, "neither agree nor disagree") using a corrected  = .05 /8 = .00625 (see Table 2 and Figure 3).

Study 2 participants did not perceive the average nonbinary person as particularly feminine, insofar as mean perceived femininity was at the scale midpoint.
However, perceived masculinity was on average fairly substantially below the scale midpoint.
The distribution of perceived femininity was centered around the midpoint, whereas the distribution of perceived masculinity was shifted toward the lower half of the scale (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: The distribution of perceived femininity was centered around the midpoint, whereas the distribution of perceived masculinity was shifted toward the lower half of the scale (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>).

text.text: Interestingly, this pattern does not straightforwardly suggest the average nonbinary person is viewed as androgynous or gender-neutral, given the lower-than-midpoint ratings of masculinity.
This pattern may reflect the notion that masculinity is more strongly enforced than femininity (Vandello et al., 2008).
text.formatted: This pattern may reflect the notion that masculinity is more strongly enforced than femininity <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Vandello et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Manhood is not automatically conferred to men; rather, it must be earned and upheld by enacting masculinity and avoiding femininity (Vandello et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Manhood is not automatically conferred to men; rather, it must be earned and upheld by enacting masculinity and avoiding femininity <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Vandello et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, womanhood is not fragile or precarious in this manner and (once conferred) it need not be continuously enacted to the same extent as manhood (Vandello & Bosson, 2013).
text.formatted: In contrast, womanhood is not fragile or precarious in this manner and (once conferred) it need not be continuously enacted to the same extent as manhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Vandello & Bosson, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, cisgender perceivers might be unlikely to attribute high levels of masculinity to nonbinary people.

Indirectly supporting this interpretation, Perez-Arche and Miller (2021) found that whereas greater prejudice toward nonbinary people was associated with stronger endorsement of traditional male gender roles, endorsement of traditional female gender roles predicted lesser prejudice.
However, given that the pattern of below-midpoint perceived masculinity was not specifically predicted, Study 3 sought to replicate this result in a non-student sample.
Study 2 additionally revealed that the attribution of gendered traits to the average nonbinary person did not follow the pattern observed in prior work on binary gender stereotypes.

Instead, cisgender perceivers attributed a mixture of feminine and masculine traits to the average nonbinary person, with the two most strongly attributed traits being emotional (a stereotypically feminine trait) and independent (a stereotypically masculine trait).
Stereotypes of nonbinary people may thus represent a unique trait profile -people who are emotional, kind, not dominant or aggressive, yet also independent and not passive.
Study 3 sought to replicate this pattern as well.
Study 3 provided a replication of Study 2 among a sample of U.S. adults recruited from CloudResearch Connect (Hartman et al., 2023).

text.text: The primary goal was to examine whether the below-midpoint ratings of masculinity of the average nonbinary person would emerge in a sample that was more diverse in terms of age, background, and geographical location than the Study 2 student sample.

Study 3 additionally provided an opportunity to explore perceptions of femininity and masculinity among a subsample of participants who endorsed very negative attitudes toward nonbinary people as inferred from open-ended responses.

text.text: A sample of 277 yielded 80% power to detect Cohen's d = 0.17 in a one-sample ttest (two-tailed, α = .05).

Familiarity with the term gender nonbinary (M = 3.26, SD = 0.96), perceived femininity ( = .89), perceived masculinity ( = .89), gendered trait attribution, and attitudes toward nonbinary people ( = .97, M = 4.84, SD = 1.69) were assessed as in Study 2.

The procedure was identical to Study 2 with three exceptions: Data were collected through CloudResearch Connect rather than from college students; the additional individual difference measures included in Study 2 (see Footnote 4) were not included; and just before providing demographic information, participants responded to the following open-ended question: "If you had to define gender nonbinary identity in your own words, what would you say?"
Examination of the open-ended responses suggested that most participants wrote a definition of nonbinary identity that matched how nonbinary people experience their own gender.

For example, participants defined nonbinary identity as having a gender beyond the woman/man binary (e.g., "Someone that doesn't identify solely with masculine or feminine"; "someone who doesnt [sic] identify as a man or woman"), being gender-neutral (e.g., "The person has no preference and doesnt [sic] identify as any gender, they are neutral"; "People who don't identify with any gender"), being genderfluid (e.g., "Seeing oneself as being fluid on the man/woman gender identity scale, or not on it at all"; "Just fluid.

An individual who, day to day, exhibits whatever sex they feel they are"), or defying gender norms (e.g., "People that do not follow the traditional gender norms accepted by society"; "A person who doesn't conform to the social norms of man or woman and freely express [sic] how they identify").
By contrast, a subsample of participants defined nonbinary people as being mentally ill, confused about their gender, or attention-seeking.

Prior work has revealed that cisgender respondents who define "transgender" by referring to confusion report distinctively negative attitudes toward transgender people (Anderson, 2023; Reiman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Prior work has revealed that cisgender respondents who define "transgender" by referring to confusion report distinctively negative attitudes toward transgender people <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Reiman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, these definitions in Study 3 plausibly index negative attitudes toward nonbinary people.
All definitions were then coded as either mentioning or not mentioning mental illness, confusion, and/or attention-seeking.
Of the 277 participants, 51 (18.41%) were coded into this category.

Example responses included: "I would call it a mental illness"; "a mental disability"; "Someone who is confused about their own identity so they refuse to admit what they truly are biologically"; "Confused people who are mostly attention seekers"; and "People looking for attention by rejecting their true gender."
Exploratory analyses compared these 51 participants 5 to the rest of the sample.

An exploratory factor analysis with maximum likelihood extraction and Oblimin rotation on trait attribution suggested three factors.

The traits gentle, kind, and passive loaded on factor 1 (loadings of 1.00, .64, and .36, respectively); aggressive and emotional loaded on Factor 2 (loadings of .75 and .38, respectively); and dominant and competitive loaded on factor 3 (loadings of .59 and .46, respectively).

Exploratory analyses repeated the tests reported above separately for the 51 participants (18.41% of the sample) who mentioned mental illness, confusion, or attention-seeking when defining nonbinary identity in their own words and the remaining 226 participants (81.59% of the sample) who did not mention these themes.

These analyses provided an opportunity to explore whether perceptions of the average nonbinary person differed between participants who spontaneously expressed a highly negative view of nonbinary identity and those who did not.

text.text: Thus, the trait attribution pattern observed among the full samples in Studies 2-3 was replicated only among participants who did not define nonbinary identity with reference to mental illness, confusion, or attention-seeking.

Replicating Study 2, Study 3 revealed that although straight cisgender U.S. participants did not view the average nonbinary person as especially feminine, they rated the average nonbinary person as below the scale midpoint on masculinity.

Studies 2-3 suggest that cisgender Americans may be reluctant to attribute masculinity to nonbinary people, potentially reflecting an overall tendency to more strongly enforce masculine (vs. feminine) gender norms (Vandello & Bosson, 2013).
text.formatted: Studies 2-3 suggest that cisgender Americans may be reluctant to attribute masculinity to nonbinary people, potentially reflecting an overall tendency to more strongly enforce masculine (vs. feminine) gender norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Vandello & Bosson, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Study 3 also replicated the pattern of gendered trait attribution from Study 2:
The average nonbinary person was ascribed a mixture of feminine (e.g., emotional) and masculine (e.g., independent) traits.
Open-ended data revealed a subsample of Study 3 participants who spontaneously expressed a highly negative view of nonbinary identity.
These participants also demonstrated a distinctively negative pattern in terms of the traits they attributed to the average nonbinary person.
Nonetheless, perceptions of below-midpoint masculinity were observed among all participants in Studies 2-3.
The tendency to view the average nonbinary person as relatively lower in masculinity is therefore not limited to perceivers who endorse negative opinions about nonbinary identity.
People tend to automatically encode others as women or men (Gallagher et al., 2025) and expect women to enact femininity and men to enact masculinity (Eagly & Wood, 2012).
text.formatted: People tend to automatically encode others as women or men <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gallagher et al., 2025)</ref> and expect women to enact femininity and men to enact masculinity <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Eagly & Wood, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The present work explored how nonbinary people fit into these binary expectations.
Study 1 showed no bias in cisgender U.S. perceivers' assumptions about whether the average nonbinary person is more likely to be female or male.
Studies 2-3 found no tendency for cisgender U.S. perceivers to view the average nonbinary person as particularly feminine (i.e., perceived femininity was at the scale midpoint).

However, Studies 2-3 indicated that cisgender perceivers appear reluctant or unlikely to ascribe even scale-midpoint levels of masculinity to the average nonbinary person (i.e., perceived masculinity was reliably below the midpoint).

In Study 3, the tendency to ascribe below-midpoint levels of masculinity emerged both among participants who endorsed negative attitudes toward nonbinary identity as well as among those whose attitudes were more positive.
Accordingly, this pattern is not a mere reflection of negative attitudes.
Americans report a growing awareness of nonbinary identity (Horowitz, 2025).
text.formatted: Americans report a growing awareness of nonbinary identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Horowitz, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the majority of Study 3 participants generated a definition of nonbinary identity that matched how many nonbinary people self-identify, indicating that cisgender Americans can describe nonbinary gender accurately.
That participants nonetheless did not ascribe much masculinity to the average nonbinary person is notable.

Whereas cisgender people can spontaneously express the notion that nonbinary gender may reflect a mixture of femininity and masculinity, they nonetheless tended to rate the average nonbinary person as below the scale midpoint on masculinity (and at the midpoint on femininity).
Thus, for some participants, perceptions of femininity and masculinity did not entirely match their own definitions of nonbinary identity.
This pattern might be associated with the generally strict enforcement of masculine gender norms (Vandello & Bosson, 2013).
text.formatted: This pattern might be associated with the generally strict enforcement of masculine gender norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Vandello & Bosson, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: For example, gender norms dictate that "real men" must avoid any appearance of femininity (Vandello et al., 2008).
text.formatted: For example, gender norms dictate that "real men" must avoid any appearance of femininity <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Vandello et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, gender norms for women are relatively less rigid (Bosson et al., 2022; Sczesny et al., 2025).
text.formatted: By contrast, gender norms for women are relatively less rigid <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bosson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Sczesny et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Masculinity is thus a valued characteristic that is not easily or automatically granted to men.
Refraining from perceiving even at-midpoint levels of masculinity in nonbinary people might reflect this overall tendency to reserve masculinity primarily for those deemed "real men."

The pattern of relatively low masculinity and midpoint-levels of femininity attributed to the average nonbinary person may speak to prior findings that nonbinary gender is perceived as less "real" than binary gender identities (McCarty & Burt, 2024; Valen & Burke, 2025).
text.formatted: The pattern of relatively low masculinity and midpoint-levels of femininity attributed to the average nonbinary person may speak to prior findings that nonbinary gender is perceived as less "real" than binary gender identities <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(McCarty & Burt, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Valen & Burke, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Perceiving gender appears to be critical to perceiving humanness, such that targets who are not assigned a specific gender are rated as less human compared to targets who are described as female or male (Martin & Mason, 2022).
text.formatted: Perceiving gender appears to be critical to perceiving humanness, such that targets who are not assigned a specific gender are rated as less human compared to targets who are described as female or male <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Martin & Mason, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that nonbinary gender identity is deemed invalid or "not real" because nonbinary people are not perceived as either clearly feminine or clearly masculine.
Future research might test this possibility directly.

Studies 2-3 additionally revealed that traits that are typically selectively attributed to women or men did not follow the same factor structure when participants considered how they might apply to nonbinary people.
Instead, the average nonbinary person was ascribed a profile of traits consisting of both stereotypically feminine (e.g., emotional) and masculine (e.g., independent) characteristics.
One possibility is that nonbinary people are viewed as akin to
LGBTQ+ rights activists.

The joint attribution of traits such as emotional and independent might thus reflect characteristics that are stereotypically ascribed to activists from marginalized groups, which tend to signal strength and emotional reactivity (Burrows et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The joint attribution of traits such as emotional and independent might thus reflect characteristics that are stereotypically ascribed to activists from marginalized groups, which tend to signal strength and emotional reactivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Burrows et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In general, the present studies are consistent with the notion that femininity and masculinity are not the endpoints of one continuum (Hester et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In general, the present studies are consistent with the notion that femininity and masculinity are not the endpoints of one continuum <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hester et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Rather, people are perceived as possessing varying levels of both femininity and masculinity.
Despite providing insight into how straight cisgender Americans think about nonbinary gender, the present studies have limitations that must be considered when interpreting the findings.

First, it is important to emphasize that the present work examined how straight cisgender respondents think about the overall category of nonbinary people and cannot speak to how specific nonbinary persons might be perceived.

For example, perceptions of a nonbinary target person (e.g., based on a photograph or actual social interaction) as feminine or masculine are likely in part determined by the particular gender expression (e.g., appearance, clothing) of the individual being perceived.
Additionally, prior work has shown that attitudes toward genderdiverse populations differ as a function of whether the social context is gender-segregated or gender-integrated.

In particular, straight cisgender Americans report more negative attitudes toward transgender people when considering gender-segregated life domains such as restrooms or locker rooms, compared to gender-integrated life domains such as education and employment (Buck & Obzud, 2018).
text.formatted: In particular, straight cisgender Americans report more negative attitudes toward transgender people when considering gender-segregated life domains such as restrooms or locker rooms, compared to gender-integrated life domains such as education and employment <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Buck & Obzud, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Perceptions of nonbinary people's femininity and masculinity might thus be different if respondents were considering life domains that make (binary) gender salient.

Furthermore, whereas Study 2's findings regarding perceived femininity and masculinity were replicated in Study 3, Study 1's results regarding a lack of bias in terms of assumptions about assigned sex (female vs. male) would benefit from replication.
Attempts to replicate this specific finding might employ task instructions that are more succinct and thus easier to parse than the relatively wordy language used in Study 1.

In general, future work ought to examine whether cisgender people possess a perceptual category of "gender nonbinary" or whether all targets are spontaneously categorized as either women or men (regardless of their actual gender identity), and how such perceptual processes relate to targets' gender expression and the contextual salience of gender.

Second, participants reported on their perceptions of the average nonbinary person in isolation, without direct comparisons to targets with binary gender identities (whether cisgender or transgender).

On one hand, this design provides insight into what comes to mind most immediately when cisgender people consider the average nonbinary person, thereby perhaps illustrating parts of the prototype of the category "nonbinary people."

On the other hand, asking participants to rate their perceptions of the femininity and masculinity of nonbinary people as well as women and men would provide comparative information that the present studies lack.
Future studies would do well to use within-subjects designs of this kind.
Third, specific identities that fall under the nonbinary umbrella term might result in distinct patterns of perceived femininity and masculinity.
People who identify as gender-neutral, agender, genderfluid, or genderqueer are plausibly perceived differently from one another.
Additionally, nonbinary individuals who use they/them pronouns or neopronouns (e.g., fae/fem, ze/zir) may also evoke distinct patterns of gender perception and gendered trait attribution.
Future research might productively address these possibilities.

Fourth, although it is possible to speculate about the implications of how nonbinary people are perceived in terms of femininity and masculinity, the task of directly examining these consequences must be taken up in future studies.
For example, are nonbinary people seen as less human, or is their gender identity invalidated, as a function of the levels of femininity and masculinity attributed to them?
Under what circumstances do cisgender people view nonbinary people as more or less gendered?
Answers to such questions would help elucidate how people perceive gender in general (Martin & Slepian, 2025).
text.formatted: Answers to such questions would help elucidate how people perceive gender in general <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Martin & Slepian, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Fifth, the present data came from primarily straight cisgender U.S. residents.
As such, all patterns are limited to the U.S. cultural context.

There is considerable cultural variation in the prevalence of genders that exist outside the binary, and it remains entirely possible that nonbinary people are perceived systematically differently across cultures.

Importantly, the present samples are also not representative of the U.S. Associations between dependent measures and participant demographic characteristics are reported in Supplemental Materials and indicate that only participant gender and political conservatism consistently correlated with perceptions of the average nonbinary person (with men, relative to women, ascribing more femininity and less masculinity, and more conservative participants attributing more negative traits).
Moreover, Democrats (vs.
Republicans) were overrepresented in the present work.
The current U.S. political landscape frequently uses gender identity as a wedge issue, and Americans' views on gender identity are strongly politically polarized (Pew Research Center, 2025).
text.formatted: The current U.S. political landscape frequently uses gender identity as a wedge issue, and Americans' views on gender identity are strongly politically polarized <ref type="bibr">(Pew Research Center, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As such, the imbalance in terms of political party affiliation may complicate the interpretation of the present results, despite the presence of a subsample of participants in Study 3 who were clearly relatively conservative in terms of their views on nonbinary gender.
More broadly speaking, as politics change at the societal level, so too might perceptions of nonbinary people at the individual level.

Accordingly, in addition to being limited to nonrepresentative samples of straight cisgender Democrat-leaning U.S.-based perceivers, the patterns observed here may reflect the specifics of a particular sociopolitical moment.
Gender identity diversity has increased in the U.S. and worldwide, especially among younger generations (Brown, 2022; Horowitz, 2025).
text.formatted: Gender identity diversity has increased in the U.S. and worldwide, especially among younger generations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Horowitz, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Many cisgender perceivers nonetheless expect everyone to have a binary gender identity (Public Religion Research Institute, 2023) and to enact their gender as either clearly feminine-presenting or masculine-presenting (Martin & Slepian, 2020 , 2025).
text.formatted: Many cisgender perceivers nonetheless expect everyone to have a binary gender identity <ref type="bibr">(Public Religion Research Institute, 2023)</ref> and to enact their gender as either clearly feminine-presenting or masculine-presenting <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Martin & Slepian, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Nonbinary people explicitly defy these expectations and are thus likely to face backlash.
The present work suggests that straight cisgender perceivers in the U.S. have specific assumptions about the femininity and masculinity of the average nonbinary person.
A particular nonbinary individual may or may not meet these assumptions, suggesting another potential avenue for backlash to emerge.

People who work with nonbinary individuals (e.g., healthcare providers, social workers, educators) should be aware of their own assumptions and the potential for bias stemming from deep-seated beliefs about the nature of gender and gendered characteristics.
More broadly, understanding the ascription of femininity and masculinity to individuals who do not conform to traditional binary genders is key to ensuring gender equality.

Do straight cisgender respondents attribute traditionally feminine and/or masculine traits to the average nonbinary person?
One-sample t-tests compared the attribution of each trait against the scale midpoint (4, "neither agree nor disagree").
A corrected  = .05 /8 = .00625 was employed for these analyses.
Results are reported in the table below.
Straight cisgender participants in Study 2 rated the average nonbinary person as relatively high (i.e., reliably above the midpoint) on emotionality, independence, kindness, and gentleness.
Ratings of competitiveness and passivity were not reliably different from the midpoint.
Although ratings of dominance and aggressiveness were below the scale midpoint, these comparisons did not survive Bonferroni correction in this smaller subsample.
Otherwise, all patterns reported in the main text replicated in this smaller subsample of Study 2 participants who reported being straight/heterosexual.
